speaker: mikebrownlee
text: Good morning, Your Honors. May it please the court. My name is Mike Brownlee. I'm here on behalf of the appellate, Robert Olinger. And so, Your Honors, this is a foreclosure appeal, as you know. The issue on appeal is whether the trust introduced sufficient evidence at trial to establish that it had standing at the inception of the suit at the time it filed its complaint. Our position is the trust failed to carry its burden of proof at trial, and here's why. We've got, when the trust filed its complaint, it attached a copy of Mr. Olinger's note that does not have any endorsements. Then about a year later, the trust files the purported original of the same note, and it does contain endorsements. And this court's decision in Madel and other decisions that we cited in the briefs make clear that under these circumstances, for the trust to establish standing, it needed to elicit testimony at trial to explain the discrepancy between the copy of the note and the original, and to prove that it actually had possession of the endorsed version of the note at the time the complaint was filed.

speaker: kimmello
text: Thank you. Good morning, may I please the court? My name is Kim Mello and I represent the trustee in this matter. As council stated, this issue and this appeal is whether the trustee presented substantial competent evidence of its standing to foreclose at the time the complaint was filed. I think the standard here is important. It is competent, substantial evidence. This court is not here to reweigh the evidence and act as a fact finder. That's already been done by the trial court. So the role here is just to determine whether or not there is in fact legally sufficient evidence in this record. And you'll find these in numerous foreclosure cases. This is not an unusual situation where the copy of the note that is attached to the complaint is not endorsed. And sometimes you'll have situations where there's actually no note that's attached to the complaint and the endorsed note is later produced and it is admitted into evidence at trial. When you have this situation, there's two things that the plaintiff has to prove. One of them is that the original note was endorsed prior to the complaint being filed. And the second thing that the plaintiff has to prove is that the trustee or its agent had physical possession prior to the filing of the complaint. So those are two things that the courts say have to be proven. And that's just based on the UCC definition of what constitutes holder status. It's those two things that are controlling. Under this court's precedent, the trustee clearly met its burden. Marciano is controlling. And in that case, there was no note attached, but the evidence that was adduced at trial in Marciano, very similar to this case. You have the original endorsed note, you have the pooling and servicing agreement, and you have the mortgage loan schedule. Those all were also introduced into evidence in this case. In this case, the pooling and servicing agreement was admitted without objection. The plaintiff is clearly the trustee under the PSA. The PSA contains the key section 2.01 language, which requires that there be a chain of endorsements from the original lender. And then that chain of endorsement end with the note being endorsed and blank. And also in the section 2.01 language, saying that the mortgage loans, okay, have to be placed into the trust as of the closing date. The closing date in this case was April 1 of 2006. In addition, like Marciano, the witness did testify on this issue. And the testimony was pretty clear. I mean, it's at page 52 to 53. Of the transcript itself and what the witness said, the questions, the two key questions, and these were her answers. It was, and this loan was included in the trust prior to the closing date, pursuant to the testimony relying on the MLS, the mortgage loan schedule, is that correct? That is correct, yes, was the witness's answer. So therefore we know that the note must have been endorsed before the suit was filed, correct? And she says, that is correct, yes. So based on the pooling and servicing agreement, which had the section 2.01 language, based on the mortgage loan schedule, which listed the borrower's loan, and based on the witness testimony, which confirmed that in fact, the loan had been placed into the trust in 2006, which was three years before the filing of the complaint, that was competent, substantial evidence of standing. This court in Marciano said that the PSA demonstrated that it had, and when I say PSA, it's the pooling and servicing agreement, demonstrated that it had possession of the blank endorsed note at the time the complaint was filed. And the court looked to the witness testimony that made clear that the loan became a trust asset prior to closing, and that it predated the complaint. So from our standpoint, Marciano is controlling, it's on point, and really, I mean, it really can't be distinguished. The borrower heavily relies on the Medall case, also out of the fifth DCA. And there's three key differences between Marciano and the Medall case. So in Medall, you have witness testimony where the witness clearly did not know when the endorsement had been placed on the note. Okay, here, based on the testimony that I just described, that's not an issue here. We did have witness testimony of when the endorsement was placed on the note, relying on the PSA.

speaker: mikebrownlee
text: Your honors, I think what's important to keep in mind here is that just let's assume for the sake of argument that the trust established that this loan was included in the trust. You still have to prove that you have possession of the endorsed note. And I'll read a quote from Perez, which is out of the fourth DCA. Evidence that the note was physically transferred into a trust prior to Deutsche Bank filing its foreclosure complaint is not by itself established standing. A plaintiff must prove not only physical possession of the original note, but also if the plaintiff is not the named payee, possession of the original note endorsed in favor of the plaintiff or in blank. So our position is that the PSA and the MLS are much new about nothing unless the trust is able to point to evidence that shows they had physical possession of not just a note or a copy of the note, but the endorsed version of the original. And I think that's dispositive here, at least in terms of the trust reliance on the PSA and the MLS. And I'd also remind the court, the standard of review is de novo.
